section.title: His Steadfast Love Endures Forever
section.sectionRationale: The climactic psalm of the Egyptian Hallel sung at Passover, this song of thanksgiving contains the most explicitly messianic verses of the whole collection, the rejected stone become the cornerstone and the cry of Hosanna, both quoted directly of Jesus at His triumphal entry.
section.thesis: The LORD whose steadfast love endures forever delivers His afflicted one from every surrounding enemy and death itself, exalting the very stone the builders rejected to become the cornerstone, the day of the LORD's own marvelous doing.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the opening call to give thanks, echoed by Israel, the priesthood, and all who fear the LORD, verses 1-4; refuge in the LORD proven better than trust in man, verses 5-9; victory over surrounding nations in the LORD's name, verses 10-14; life preserved to declare the LORD's deeds, verses 15-18; entering the gates of righteousness, verses 19-21; the rejected stone become the cornerstone and the cry of Hosanna, verses 22-27; and the closing return to thanksgiving, verses 28-29.

units.label: His loving devotion endures forever
units.note: the call to give thanks, echoed three times

verses.text: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.
Let Israel say, "His loving devotion endures forever."
Let the house of Aaron say, "His loving devotion endures forever."
Let those who fear the LORD say, "His loving devotion endures forever."

units.label: Better to take refuge in the LORD
units.note: than to trust in man or princes

verses.text: In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered and set me free.
The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?
The LORD is on my side; He is my helper. Therefore I will look in triumph on those who hate me.
It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man.
It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.

units.label: In the name of the LORD I cut them off

verses.text: All the nations surrounded me, but in the name of the LORD I cut them off.
They surrounded me on every side, but in the name of the LORD I cut them off.
They swarmed around me like bees, but they were extinguished like burning thorns; in the name of the LORD I cut them off.
I was pushed so hard I was falling, but the LORD helped me.
The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation.

units.label: I will not die, but I will live
units.note: life preserved to declare God's deeds

verses.text: Shouts of joy and salvation resound in the tents of the righteous: "The right hand of the LORD performs with valor!
The right hand of the LORD is exalted! The right hand of the LORD performs with valor!"
I will not die, but I will live and proclaim what the LORD has done.
The LORD disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death.

units.label: Open to me the gates of righteousness

verses.text: Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter and give thanks to the LORD.
This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it.
I will give You thanks, for You have answered me, and You have become my salvation.

units.label: The stone the builders rejected
units.note: the cornerstone, and Hosanna, cited of Christ

verses.text: The {{even_pinnah|stone}} the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.
This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes.
This is the day that the LORD has made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
O LORD, save us, we pray. We beseech You, O LORD, cause us to prosper!
Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. From the house of the LORD we bless you.
The LORD is God; He has made His light to shine upon us. Bind the festal sacrifice with cords to the horns of the altar.

units.label: You are my God, and I will give You thanks

verses.text: You are my God, and I will give You thanks. You are my God, and I will exalt You.
Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.

even_pinnah.gloss: The cornerstone, literally the head of the corner, the foundational stone that aligns and bears the weight of an entire structure. What builders discarded as unfit becomes, by God's own doing, the very stone the whole building depends on, quoted directly of Jesus in Matthew 21:42, Acts 4:11, and 1 Peter 2:7.

basic.context: This climactic psalm of the Passover Hallel moves a rescued worshiper, likely the king, from a cry in distress, through victory over surrounding enemies who swarmed like bees, to entering the temple gates in thanksgiving, and finally to the psalm's two most explosive lines, a rejected stone become the cornerstone and a cry of Hosanna for the one who comes in the LORD's name.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's refrain, His loving devotion endures forever, framing the whole song, verses 1-4 and 29, teaches that every deliverance recounted here, from surrounding nations, from near death, from rejection, flows from God's unchanging covenant love, not from the worshiper's own merit.
basic.originalLanguages: The stone the builders rejected becomes the even pinnah, literally rosh pinnah, the head of the corner, verse 22, the foundational stone bearing the whole building's weight. Verse 25's cry, O LORD, save us, we pray, is the Hebrew hoshia na, which becomes the Greek Hosanna shouted at Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, Matthew 21:9.
basic.typology: The rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone, verse 22, is quoted by Jesus of Himself after the parable of the vineyard, Matthew 21:42, by Peter before the Sanhedrin, Acts 4:11, and by Peter again describing all believers as living stones built on Him, 1 Peter 2:4-7; and the blessing on him who comes in the name of the LORD, verse 26, is shouted by the crowds at the Triumphal Entry, Matthew 21:9.
basic.christ: This is the climactic Hallel Psalm Jesus and His disciples almost certainly sang together at the Last Supper, Matthew 26:30, on the very night He would be rejected like the stone this psalm describes. Jesus applies verse 22 directly to Himself, the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, Matthew 21:42, and the crowds at His Triumphal Entry shout verse 26's Hosanna and blessing directly over Him, Matthew 21:9, so that His whole path, rejection, cornerstone exaltation, and public acclamation, is traced by this single ancient psalm.
basic.god: God is the one whose steadfast love never ends, who becomes strength, song, and salvation for the afflicted, who disciplines severely yet does not give over to death, and who Himself, marvelously, exalts what human builders discard, making the very day of that reversal a day to rejoice in.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 21:42 and Acts 4:11 apply the rejected stone directly to Jesus. Matthew 21:9 records the crowds shouting this psalm's Hosanna and blessing at the Triumphal Entry. 1 Corinthians 15:25 and Hebrews 13:6 echo this psalm's confidence in the LORD's help and eventual, total victory.
basic.oneStory: A worshiper rescued from surrounding enemies and near death enters the temple gates in thanksgiving to celebrate a rejected stone becoming the cornerstone, a psalm that traces, centuries in advance, the whole shape of Christ's path, rejected by builders, hailed with Hosanna, and exalted by God's own marvelous doing to become the very foundation on which His whole church now stands.

context.literary:
Psalm 118 is built like a liturgy, and its voices change as the worshippers move. It opens with a call to thanks that Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD answer one after another, verses 1 to 4. Then a single voice testifies, verses 5 to 18, and the testimony widens in three rings of danger: a personal one in verses 5 to 9, where the speaker is in a tight place and no human helper is needed; a national one in verses 10 to 12, where the nations swarm round on every side; and a mortal one in verses 13 to 18, where he is pushed so hard he is falling and nearly dies. Each ring ends in rescue, and each rescue is credited to the LORD.

At verse 19 the scene changes to a threshold. The speaker asks for the gates to open, and a second voice, most likely a priest or gatekeeper, answers in verse 20. Verses 22 to 24 read like the congregation's response in the courts, with plural 'we' and 'our eyes'. Verses 25 to 27 are petition and blessing, spoken from the house itself, and verse 28 is one more personal vow. Verse 29 repeats verse 1, so the psalm ends where it began.

The devices serve the argument. Verses 6 and 7 repeat 'The LORD is on my side'. Verses 8 and 9 are twin proverbs that set the LORD against man, then against princes. Verses 10 to 12 repeat one refrain three times, and verses 15 and 16 name the 'right hand of the LORD' three times. Repetition is how a crowd learns a song, and this psalm was meant to be sung by a crowd.
context.historical:
The psalm closes the Egyptian Hallel, Psalms 113 to 118, so called because Psalm 114 recalls the exodus. Jewish practice later divided the Hallel around the Passover meal, and the psalm was also sung at the other pilgrim feasts. The mention of tents in verse 15, the boughs and the procession at the altar in verse 27, and the shouting of 'save us' all fit the Feast of Tabernacles, when the people were told to rejoice with palm branches and the boughs of leafy trees, Leviticus 23:40. John records the crowd at the Triumphal Entry with palm branches, John 12:13.

The date is not stated. The speaker speaks as a leader whose rescue is the whole nation's, and the refrain 'He is good; His loving devotion endures forever' was already a stock phrase of temple praise under David and Jehoshaphat, 1 Chronicles 16:34 and 2 Chronicles 20:21. The same words rang out when the foundation of the second temple was laid, Ezra 3:10 to 11, and some readers place the psalm in that rebuilding. Zechariah's picture of the capstone brought out 'accompanied by shouts of Grace, grace to it,' Zechariah 4:7, belongs to the same moment.

The stone image would have been familiar to anyone who had seen a building site. A builder who inspects a stone and sets it aside may later find that it is the one the whole corner depends on. Whether the 'head of the corner' is a foundation stone that fixes the angle of two walls or a stone set at the top where they meet, the picture is of one piece that holds the others together, and the surprise is that the experts overlooked it.
context.canonical:
The psalm draws on the Torah's songs and gives them back to Israel. Verse 14 is Exodus 15:2 almost word for word, 'The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation,' and Isaiah 12:2 takes it up again for the day of final rescue. Verses 8 and 9 are the same teaching as Psalm 146:3, Jeremiah 17:5 and Psalm 20:7: do not trust in princes, in man, or in chariots.

The stone has a long life in the prophets. Isaiah 28:16 has the LORD laying 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation,' while Isaiah 8:14 has the same LORD becoming 'a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.' Daniel sees a stone cut without human hands that crushes a statue, Daniel 2:34.

The New Testament quotes this psalm more than almost any other. Jesus ends the parable of the tenants with verses 22 and 23, Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10 to 11 and Luke 20:17. Peter says before the council that this Jesus is that stone, Acts 4:11, and applies it again in 1 Peter 2:7. Paul calls Christ 'the cornerstone' of the household of God, Ephesians 2:20. The cry of verse 26 greets Jesus at the Triumphal Entry, Matthew 21:9 and John 12:13, and Jesus himself uses it as the condition of his return, Matthew 23:39. Hebrews 13:6 lifts verse 6 straight into the confession of Christians.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wanted the festival crowd to rehearse a particular order of events: distress, cry, rescue, entry, thanks. It is a pattern for worship, and the speaker's own story is told so that every pilgrim who files through the gate can say it with him. That is why a personal testimony is set inside a choir's refrain.

He also meant to settle where security lies. The two proverbs of verses 8 and 9 sit exactly between the first testimony and the battle account, and everything around them proves the point: the nations are many and the LORD is enough. Rescue in this psalm is never earned. The speaker admits he was falling, verse 13, and he admits the LORD's discipline, verse 18, and then he gives all the credit away.

The verses about the stone are an answer to humiliation. Whoever the speaker was, he or his people had been judged and set aside by the powerful, and the author wants Israel to see that God's verdict reverses human verdicts. The joy of verse 24 is the joy of a people who have been vindicated by someone other than themselves.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes one worshipper's deliverance and a festival liturgy. It does not promise that every rejected person will be lifted up in this life, nor that every enemy will be cut down as these verses report. The language of triumph over the nations comes from a king's military experience and cannot simply be borrowed as a charter for violence.

What the psalm does prescribe is a posture. Believers are told to give thanks on the basis of God's character rather than their circumstances, and to say so together, verses 1 to 4. They are told to take refuge in the LORD rather than in influence, verses 8 and 9. And they are told to approach God through the way he has opened, with a prayer for the gates and with thanks, verses 19 to 21. For Christians the cornerstone verses are first of all a statement about Jesus, which the New Testament makes for us, and only then a comfort for the rejected. Peter does the second step carefully in 1 Peter 2:4 to 5, where those who come to the living stone become living stones themselves.

debates.question: Who is the original historical speaker of this psalm, the one surrounded by nations and later entering the temple gates?

views.label: A Davidic king celebrating a military deliverance
views.case: The first person is a leader whose personal rescue involves all the nations, verses 10 to 12, and whose entry through the gate sets off a choir. Royal thanksgiving of this kind appears in Psalm 18 and Psalm 20. The processional shape suits a king leading the people into the sanctuary.

views.label: The restored community speaking as one voice
views.case: Corporate speech is common in the psalm, 'Let Israel say,' and the stone that was rejected and then set in place fits a people who were scorned by their neighbours and brought back to rebuild. Ezra 3:10 to 11 uses the same refrain at the laying of the foundation.

views.label: A festival worshipper who stands in for the whole people
views.case: Because the psalm was sung at the feasts, the 'I' may have been designed from the start to be spoken by every pilgrim, so that no single historical figure needs to be named.

debates.bearing: Whoever first spoke, the New Testament treats verses 22 to 26 as speaking of the Messiah, and a psalm that was written for any worshipper to sing is a fitting vehicle for that. Readers who prefer a single original speaker still find the psalm's pattern of rejection, rescue and entry fulfilled in Jesus.

debates.question: What does 'This is the day that the LORD has made' refer to in verse 24?

views.label: The day of the temple festival or entry
views.case: In the liturgy the 'day' is the day of the feast itself, when the gates are opened and the congregation rejoices. 'This' points at the occasion being celebrated, and the verb 'made' here means God has appointed it.

views.label: The day of the stone's reversal in verses 22 and 23
views.case: Hebrew 'this' in verse 23 is feminine, and the next verse repeats it, so many see verses 22 to 24 as one unit: the day is the day God turns rejection around. The church has long sung the verse on Easter morning for that reason.

debates.bearing: Both readings keep the same centre, that the day is God's making and not man's. The second becomes richly Christian when the stone's reversal is the resurrection, as in Acts 4:10 to 11, but the first stops us from reading the psalm as if it had no original festival setting.

debates.question: What is the festal offering of verse 27 bound with?

views.label: Sacrificial animals tied with cords to the altar's horns
views.case: The BSB follows this reading, 'Bind the festal sacrifice with cords to the horns of the altar.' It matches the practice of tethering the victim at the altar, and the horns of the altar appear in Exodus 27:2 as its corners.

views.label: A procession carrying boughs up to the altar
views.case: The BSB footnote offers 'Join in the festal procession with boughs in hand, up to the horns of the altar.' The word for festival may also mean a pilgrim procession, and boughs belong to Tabernacles, Leviticus 23:40.

debates.bearing: The grammar is hard and neither reading changes the doctrine. Either the people bring a thank offering to the altar or they dance towards it holding branches. What is certain is that the psalm ends at the altar, where thanks becomes visible.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 5 turns on a contrast of places. The speaker says he called from the metsar, a narrow strait, and that the LORD answered in the merchav, a wide open place, which the BSB renders 'set me free.' Distress in Hebrew is often a tight space and rescue a broad one, and the psalm uses the two words as bookends. The same pair stands behind Psalm 120:1, where the pilgrim's tight place is only the beginning of the road.

Verse 6 is 'The LORD is on my side' in the BSB, but the footnote gives 'Or The LORD is with me,' and the Hebrew is literally 'the LORD is for me.' The same preposition governs the claim in verse 7. The Greek of Hebrews 13:6 renders the sense as 'helper.' The speaker's boldness rests on having God as his advocate, and not merely as an observer.

In verses 10 to 12 the speaker says three times that he 'cut them off in the name of the LORD,' using one verb each time. The repetition is the point: the same outcome follows each time the nations surround him. Verse 12 adds that the enemies 'were extinguished like burning thorns.' Thorns flare brightly and then die at once, a picture of a threat that looks fierce and is gone in a moment.

Verse 14 uses the short form of God's name, Yah, which Exodus 15:2 uses in the same line, 'my strength and my song.' The psalm has now moved from a personal rescue to the oldest song of Israel's salvation, the Red Sea, so the worshipper joins his small rescue to the great one. Verse 18 uses the intensive pairing of an infinitive with a finite verb, the same construction as Genesis 2:17, so 'disciplined me severely' is more literally 'disciplining, the LORD disciplined me.' The same doubling is applied to the sentence of discipline, and then the verse insists that it was not a sentence of death.

The gates in verse 19 are 'gates of righteousness,' and the word in verse 20 for those who enter, tsaddiqim, are the 'righteous.' The psalm does not say that the entrants are sinless, since verse 18 has just spoken of discipline, but that they come on God's terms. In verse 22 the 'builders' are the Hebrew bonim, and the wordplay with even, stone, and ben, son, has often been noticed. In verse 25 the two petitions are separate verbs, the first being hoshia, save, from which the cry hoshia na, rendered Hosanna in Greek, is formed, and the second hatslichah, cause us to prosper.

Verse 26 has a singular, 'he who comes,' and a plural, 'we bless you,' both within one line. Verse 27 says the LORD 'made His light to shine upon us,' using the verb of the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:25, which suggests that this line is the people's reply to the priests' blessing.

typology.type: The gates of righteousness, verses 19 to 20
typology.fulfillment: The speaker asks that the gates be opened so that he can enter and give thanks, and the answer is that only the righteous may come through. The psalm leaves open how a person is made fit. In Christ the answer is given: He is 'the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6, and 'No one comes to the Father except through Me.' The gate image also lies behind Psalm 24:7 to 10, where the King of Glory enters. The type falls short because the temple gates admitted worshippers for a feast, while Christ opens the way into God's presence for good, Hebrews 10:19 to 20.

typology.type: The one disciplined but not given over to death, verses 17 to 18
typology.fulfillment: The speaker says he is not going to die but live, and he proclaims what the LORD has done. His near death was real, and so was his survival. The correspondence in Christ is greater: He did die, and God raised Him, 'releasing Him from the agony of death,' Acts 2:24, and He is Himself 'the resurrection and the life,' John 11:25. Paul uses the same shape of experience of the apostles, 'punished, yet not killed,' 2 Corinthians 6:9. The type falls short because the psalmist's reprieve postponed his death, while Christ's resurrection defeats it.

typology.type: The festival procession of verses 26 to 27
typology.fulfillment: The people welcome a coming one and move together with branches towards the altar. On the Sunday before His death the crowd greeted Jesus with palm branches and the words of verse 26, John 12:13, and Luke records 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord,' Luke 19:38. The correspondence is deliberate and the irony is deep, because the procession climbs towards an altar on which this king will be the sacrifice. The type falls short in that the festival crowd could not see where the procession led, and the same crowd's praise would turn within days.

typology.type: The thanksgiving offering at the altar, verse 27
typology.fulfillment: Thanks is not left as words; it is bound with cords at the horns of the altar, where a life is given. In the New Testament believers are told to offer 'a sacrifice of praise,' and the Lamb who was slain receives the praise of heaven, Revelation 5:12. The correspondence rests on thanks always being costly and mediated. The type falls short because the animal on the altar could not take away sin, whereas Christ offered Himself once for all.

study.christ:
Jesus does not borrow this psalm only for one proof text. He sings it. The Hallel was sung at the Passover meal, and Matthew and Mark both note that after the supper 'they had sung a hymn' and went out to the Mount of Olives, Matthew 26:30 and Mark 14:26. On the night of His betrayal the verses about a gate, a cornerstone and a festal altar were on His lips, and so were the verses about distress, 'The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid.'

The psalm leads to Christ along the line of the rejected and vindicated one. Mark places the first prediction of the Passion in these terms: the Son of Man 'must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes,' Mark 8:31. The verb behind 'rejected' there is the one the Greek Old Testament and Peter use for rejecting after inspection, so the builders are the very leaders who examined Him and set Him aside. Peter says the rest of the verse to those same leaders, 'whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead,' Acts 4:10 to 11. The stone is not a metaphor for general suffering, but for a particular person whom God has put in place by raising Him.

The psalm also leads to Christ by the cry of verse 25 and the blessing of verse 26. When the crowds shouted 'Hosanna' and 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord,' they were using a prayer for rescue as a greeting for a king, Matthew 21:9. Jesus makes the verse into a promise as well as a welcome: 'you will not see Me again until you say, Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord,' Matthew 23:39.

The discipline of verse 18 should be read with care. It does not mean that Christ was punished for His own sin, since He 'was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. Rather, the shape of the verse, severe suffering that does not end in death, is fulfilled in a deeper way, because He did die and was raised. Hebrews 5:7 says He 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard.' That is verse 5 of this psalm lived out.

And it leads to Christ as the cornerstone of a people. Paul says the household of God is 'built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone,' Ephesians 2:20. A caution is in order: not every detail of the psalm points to Jesus. The bees, the burning thorns and the horns of the altar are not coded messages. The links rest on the New Testament's own use of the psalm, and on the pattern of rejection, rescue and entry that the psalm itself sets out.
study.god:
The psalm's first claim about God is his goodness and his loving devotion, and it states both as permanent, 'endures forever,' verse 1. The Hebrew word behind 'loving devotion,' chesed, is covenant faithfulness, and the psalm makes three groups say it aloud, which suggests that it is meant to be confessed rather than merely believed. God's constancy is the ground under every other statement. The nations come and go, the speaker rises and falls, but this does not change.

God is personal and near. He answers a cry from a tight place and sets the speaker in a wide one, verse 5. He is 'on my side,' verse 6, and 'my helper,' verse 7. The psalm does not make the LORD a distant principle, because it uses 'my' and 'our' of him again and again, 'my strength and my song,' 'my salvation,' 'my God,' verses 14, 21 and 28.

He is strong. The right hand of the LORD 'performs with valor,' verses 15 and 16. The phrase belongs with the exodus, Exodus 15:6, and the psalm treats the victory of the speaker as a fresh outbreak of the same power that brought Israel out of Egypt.

He is a God who disciplines, and who restrains the discipline. Verse 18 holds two truths together: 'The LORD disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death.' The tension is real. A reader may wonder how a good God can allow harsh correction. The psalm's answer is that the discipline belongs to a father who has a goal, and the goal is that the speaker will live and proclaim what the LORD has done, verse 17. Compare Hebrews 12:10 to 11, where discipline is for sharing God's holiness.

He reverses human verdicts. The builders examine and reject; God sets the stone in the place of honour, and the people say 'This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes,' verse 23. God's glory is shown in choosing what the wise discard, 1 Corinthians 1:27 to 29.

He is holy, and the gate is his. Nobody enters of right: 'This is the gate of the LORD,' verse 20. And yet he opens it, because the one who calls 'Open to me' is answered. For worship, this psalm teaches us to begin and end with thanks, to name what the LORD has done in the first person, to bring the whole body into it, and to hold our confidence in a God who stands by us in the narrow place and sets us in the wide one.

crossReferences.note: The line of verse 14 appears here first, in Moses' song at the sea. The worshipper takes the oldest song of rescue in Israel and makes it his own, which tells us that the rescue of an individual in Psalm 118 is read as a fresh act of the exodus God.

King Jehoshaphat sends singers ahead of the army with the refrain of Psalm 118:1. The refrain is a battle song as well as a temple one, and it matches the psalm's own account of victory won in the name of the LORD, verses 10 to 12.

When the foundation of the second temple was laid, the people sang this refrain and gave a great shout. It places the psalm's praise at a building site, which is where the image of the stone and the builders belongs.

'Put not your trust in princes' is the second proverb of Psalm 118:9 in other words. The Hallel psalms around this one make the same point, so the instruction to take refuge in the LORD is a theme of the whole collection.

God lays 'a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation' in Zion. Peter joins this verse to Psalm 118:22 in 1 Peter 2:6 to 7, so that the stone is both the one God lays and the one men reject. The two passages explain each other.

The capstone is brought out amid shouts of 'Grace, grace to it,' as a mountain of difficulty becomes a plain. It shows the same joy at the setting of a stone that Psalm 118:22 to 24 describes, and the temple builder Zerubbabel stands where the speaker of the psalm might have stood.

Mark's version of the parable of the tenants ends with Psalm 118:22 to 23. The leaders understood that the parable was told against them, Mark 12:12, which shows that the stone and the builders were heard as a charge against those in charge of the temple.

Peter's use of the stone before the council turns at once into a statement about salvation, 'there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.' The psalm's 'my salvation' of verses 14 and 21 is thus attached to the name of Jesus.

The writer quotes the verse about not being afraid of man and says 'So we say with confidence.' The believers' answer to opposition is the same as the psalmist's, and it rests on the helper, not on their own strength.

Luke records the Triumphal Entry with the words of verse 26 and adds the word 'King.' The crowd's welcome identifies the one who comes as a king, and the Pharisees' demand that Jesus silence them, Luke 19:39, shows they understood what was being claimed.

Jesus quotes verse 26 as the condition of His return: 'you will not see Me again until you say, Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.' The psalm's blessing is no longer only a greeting but also a promise that Jerusalem will one day greet Him rightly.

study.oneStory:
The psalm sits at the point in Israel's story where memory of the exodus meets the hope of a restored temple. Behind it is the cry from the tight place in Egypt, Exodus 2:23, and the answer that brought a whole nation into a wide one. The song of verse 14 is Moses' song, so the psalmist is saying that the God of the sea is the God of this latest rescue too.

It also answers a question the Old Testament raises repeatedly: where should a people put its trust? The prophets and psalms keep returning to the contrast of verses 8 and 9, the LORD against man and princes, because Israel's story is full of kings who failed. The psalm gives the answer of faith, and Israel's later history shows how hard it was to keep.

Then it looks forward. The rejected stone and the blessing on the one who comes in the LORD's name become, in the Gospels, the key to the life of Jesus. He is rejected by the builders of Israel's religion, killed outside the city, and raised by the Father. The psalm that was sung at His last Passover is the psalm that explains it. The stone that was rejected does not stay in the rubbish heap; it becomes the foundation of a new temple, the church, a 'spiritual house' of living stones, 1 Peter 2:4 to 5.

The story is not finished at the Triumphal Entry. Jesus says Jerusalem will see Him again when it says the blessing, Matthew 23:39, and the book of Revelation pictures the end as a great festival in which the whole company of the redeemed praise the Lamb, Revelation 5:12 and 19:9. The refrain 'His loving devotion endures forever' comes true in the only way a refrain can: it is still being sung when the new creation begins. The gates opened to the righteous in verse 19 are fulfilled where the gates of the new Jerusalem are never shut, Revelation 21:25, and the psalm's prayer for a wide place is answered when God makes everything new.

quiz.q: What refrain opens and closes this psalm, framing the entire song?

options.text: Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever.
options.note: This refrain in verses 1 and 29 grounds every deliverance in the psalm in God's unending covenant love.

options.text: The wicked will be utterly destroyed forever.
options.note: This is not the psalm's opening and closing refrain, which instead celebrates God's enduring loving devotion.

options.text: Israel will never again face any enemy.
options.note: The psalm actually describes present enemies surrounding the speaker, not the absence of any future enemy.

options.text: The temple will stand forever without being rebuilt.
options.note: The refrain concerns God's loving devotion, not a specific claim about the temple's permanence.

quiz.q: According to verses 8-9, what is better than trusting in man or princes?

options.text: Taking refuge in the LORD.
options.note: This double declaration reorients all trust away from human power and toward God alone.

options.text: Trusting in one's own wealth and resources.
options.note: The verses specifically contrast trusting man and princes with taking refuge in the LORD, not personal wealth.

options.text: Forming alliances with foreign nations.
options.note: The verses reject reliance on human power broadly, which would include foreign alliances, in favor of refuge in the LORD.

options.text: Relying on one's own military strength.
options.note: The comparison given is refuge in the LORD versus trust in man or princes, not specifically military self-reliance.

quiz.q: What does verse 22 declare about the stone the builders rejected?

options.text: It has become the cornerstone.
options.note: This verse is quoted by Jesus of Himself and by Peter of Christ throughout the New Testament.

options.text: It was thrown into the sea and lost forever.
options.note: The verse says the opposite; the rejected stone becomes the most important stone, the cornerstone.

options.text: It was reused only as a doorstep, a minor function.
options.note: The verse specifically names it the cornerstone, the foundational stone bearing the whole structure's weight, not a minor function.

options.text: It remained rejected and was never used again.
options.note: The verse's whole force is the reversal: the once-rejected stone is now exalted as the cornerstone.

quiz.q: What Hebrew phrase in verse 25 becomes the Greek word Hosanna shouted at Jesus' Triumphal Entry?

options.text: Hoshia na, meaning save, we pray, or save now.
options.note: This cry is quoted directly in Matthew 21:9 and other Gospel accounts of the Triumphal Entry.

options.text: Shalom aleichem, meaning peace be upon you.
options.note: That is a separate Hebrew greeting, not the phrase behind Hosanna, which comes from hoshia na in verse 25.

options.text: Baruch haba, without any connection to save us.
options.note: While related blessing language appears in verse 26, the specific term Hosanna derives from hoshia na, save us, in verse 25.

options.text: Adonai roi, meaning the Lord is my shepherd.
options.note: That phrase belongs to Psalm 23, not to this psalm's Hosanna cry in verse 25.

quiz.q: How does Peter apply the cornerstone image of verse 22 in 1 Peter 2:4-7?

options.text: He describes believers as living stones built upon Christ, the rejected yet chosen and precious cornerstone.
options.note: Peter extends the psalm's cornerstone imagery to describe the church's identity as founded on Christ.

options.text: He denies any connection between this verse and Jesus.
options.note: Peter's application is a direct, explicit connection between this verse and Christ as the cornerstone.

options.text: He applies it only to the literal stones of Herod's temple.
options.note: Peter's application is theological and christological, concerning believers built on Christ, not merely literal temple architecture.

options.text: He applies it exclusively to future events with no present church application.
options.note: Peter's application is directly to the present identity of believers as living stones now, not solely a future event.

questions: This psalm's refrain, His loving devotion endures forever, frames every deliverance in the song. What deliverance in your own life do you need to reframe this week as evidence of God's unending covenant love rather than mere luck or coincidence?

The psalmist declares it is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man or princes. Where are you currently placing more confidence in human strength, status, or strategy than in God Himself?

This psalm's rejected stone becomes the cornerstone, exactly the pattern of Jesus' own rejection and exaltation. Where in your life does something that felt like rejection or failure need to be reframed in light of God's pattern of marvelous reversal?

The crowds shouted this psalm's Hosanna over Jesus at His Triumphal Entry, even as He rode toward the cross just days later. How does holding together both the joy of Hosanna and the reality of the coming cross shape your own worship this week?

Peter describes believers as living stones built on Christ the cornerstone. How does your identity as one of those living stones, part of something Christ Himself is building, change how you view your role in your local church community?

translationNotes.note: Cornerstone renders the Hebrew rosh pinnah, literally the head of the corner, the foundational stone that aligns and bears the weight of an entire structure; this verse is quoted directly of Jesus in Matthew 21:42, Acts 4:11, and 1 Peter 2:7.
Save us, we pray translates the Hebrew hoshia na, which becomes the Greek Hosanna shouted by the crowds at Jesus' Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem, Matthew 21:9, John 12:13.

Bind the festal sacrifice with cords, up to the horns of the altar may alternatively be rendered as an instruction to join the festal procession with branches in hand up to the altar, a phrase connected to the palm branches waved at Tabernacles and echoed at the Triumphal Entry, John 12:13.
